inline.s: The Whole Story of How Our Master, the Great Monk Hanshan, Was Brought Back to Caoxi and Enshrined

It is recorded with reverence that in the bingshen year of the Wanli era our Master entered Guangdong through adverse karmic conditions. The events of his life are fully set down in the stele inscriptions by such gentlemen as Xiao Xuanpu, Wu Guanwo, and Qian Shouzhi, which have already let slip no little of the truth. What I record here concerns only how his relic stupa was welcomed from Mt. Lu and brought back to Caoxi, and the whole story of the opening of the stupa and the lacquered cloth. In spreading the Dharma our Master spent half the energy of his life at Caoxi, as is fully recorded in the Record of the Restoration. In his later years he retired to rest at Wuru in Lu. In the renxu year of the Tianqi era, Qixiang, together with the hall master Ben'ang and others, earnestly begged the Master to return south. In the winter of the guihai year he entered quiescence at Caoxi. The Wuru community, and Elder Zhiwei Shan, wished to welcome the relic stupa back to Lu, and drew lots before the stupa; three times the lot read Keep. Thereupon Minister Xiao donated funds, and together with our circuit's Xia Wozhai, Prefect Zhang of Shaozhou, and monastic and lay disciples near and far, and the monks of the ten cloisters, they raised a stupa court. Elder Shan had followed the Master through the remnant of nine deaths in times of hardship, and was filial and utterly sincere; he invited the officials of Wu and Yue who had taken refuge in the Master's gate, and they sent letters to the authorities. Governor He then ordered that the Master be compelled back to Lu. That was the first month of the spring of the yichou year. In the gengchen year of the Chongzhen era I, Qixiang, filled the post of assistant prefect of Ruizhou, and entering the mountain to sweep the stupa, learned for the first time that the geomancers objected. After entering the stupa I opened it again for divination of the site. And I recalled how in the renxu year I had attended the Master at Lu, and the Master's parting verse said, A distant heart traces the flowing water; we are pledged to one who will not transmit the robe. And again he had given me a prediction before the assembly: You shall one day be a powerful official in the Ministry of War; you must repair the Cai family graves for me. In twenty years my official career has come to nothing. Since I could not lift the robe upon the stone, and could not even render the service of carrying earth, I harbored an inner shame. Then suddenly I woke to this: our Master's spirit is not yet at rest. If this piece of business were settled, would it not be far more than repairing a grave? So I undertook the southern journey with all my strength. My eldest son Cheng-ye was with me in office, and strongly urged it on. In the autumn of the guiwei year the bandits of Chu shook our neighbors, and we feared the flames of war. Our Dharma grandson Cili, Guangcheng and the rest, following my words, drew lots before the stupa; three times the lot was favorable. I gave up my post and prepared to return south, sending my son Cheng-ye to welcome the stupa in my place. There was one Yan Rui, whom I had once singled out, and whose courage and judgment both sides admired as equal to the task; he too earnestly begged to serve. So I sent him to Kang Commandery to arrange provisions, and there too the lot was Keep. The people of the capital objected: the Great Master is a man of our own district; if he could be welcomed away, are we alone unable to keep him? I had first asked my fellow provincial Liao Wenying, assistant prefect of Kang Commandery, to act as host. It happened that Liao had received orders from the provincial office to conduct business at Huai'an and was already aboard his boat, held there by the wind for nearly eighty days. Yan Rui pleaded with him, and Liao gladly consented. One evening the wind turned south, and he sent word to Yan: The wind is fair and we cannot stay; delay and you will ruin yourself. But Yan was down with dysentery and could not move. The sail went north across the river, and Yan had lost all hope. That very night a contrary wind rose in fury and drove Liao's boat back to its former mooring. Yan laid his hand upon his brow and said, It is the Master's spirit. So a proclamation was sent to the registrar of Xingzi county, who took charge of the matter, and notices were posted through the mountains, and none dared oppose. The garrison commanders Jin Guozhu of Rui and Hu Zongsheng of Kang both sent troops to escort it, with banners and drums leading it out of the mountains. Bandit alarms pressed closer each day and the river route was blocked and rough. Six boats went south, and on the way they met robbers. The passenger boats were all stopped and plundered, but the stupa boat alone caught the wind, spread its sail, and passed straight on; the grappling poles could find no hold. In this way many dangers were met, and danger ended in safety; rivers and mountains aided the favorable course. Was it not all our Master's spirit? On the second day of the middle month of winter that year the stupa boat reached the mountain. The assembly in the mountain raised a cheer like thunder, feeling that it had come down from heaven. Yan Rui and our Dharma grandson Cili told me that the stupa showed many wonders. At first, when it left the mountain and crossed the ridge, four men carried it; by the time it reached Mengli and came ashore, double the strength was barely enough. What is one to say to that? I said, The old man is displaying wonders; does he mean to appear in his flesh body? A lucky day was chosen for its enshrinement in the stupa, in the ninth month of the jiashen year. But brigands and famine came one upon another, and then came the great upheaval at Yan. My heart broke with grief; I wished to go into the mountain to look after it beforehand, but had no leisure. A commander-in-chief named Song Ji said to the monk Yuancang, The Master's fame resounds through the world; how can he be as other men? His vajra body must be free of flaw or loss; I beg that the stupa be opened for veneration. On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month the assembly was gathered and lots were drawn, and permission was given to open it. When it was opened, the bones of the Way were as if alive, seated upright and serene, neither leaning nor tilting; hair and nails had grown long; his garments were fresh and clean; the white silk sitting mat showed not the slightest blemish, and the cord of his rosary was like new. The great assembly shouted for joy and bowed in refuge; the onlookers pressed like a wall. Some days later the former Minister of Personnel Li Rixuan and Huang Kun of Shaozhou entered the mountain to share in the joy, and together they bore witness. Only then did people believe that a flesh-body mahāsattva had answered the conditions to ferry the world. In the past there was Dajian; now there is our Master. Earlier, the Zhuoxi spring had long run dry. Prefect Huang, who had set his heart on the Dharma gate, sought it out by a hundred devices. When the relic stupa was opened, the spring gushed forth of itself, answering like echo to sound. Was that by chance? I, Qixiang, together with Yu Zongyuanjiu, gathered the monastic and lay believers of the Changchun society of this prefecture and spread a great feast for the whole mountain. On the Double Ninth we entered the mountain; on the twenty-fifth we fed the monks. On the tenth day of the tenth month the lacquered cloth was applied and he was raised to the seat. The heads of the ten cloister households, the elders and seniors, the stupa master and hall master, and the Dharma-protecting laymen of the Changchun society all signed a joint petition asking our Dharma grandson Cili and the rest to keep and serve the incense and lamps of the stupa court. Master Song was first to donate fifty pieces of gold for the lacquered cloth, and he asked Master Li to compose an appeal for subscriptions. He said the stupa court's bearings were still cramped, and funds were needed for rebuilding, for incense and lamps, and for landed property. Governor Shen has already pledged a hundred pieces of gold. All of these men had a karmic tie of prajñā with our Master from former lives, and so in this final move each could put forth his own eye and hand, and raise a banner of light for a thousand autumns. With my slender strength, how fortunate am I to have met this occasion in person. So I record its whole story thus. A lucky day in the tenth month of the seventeenth year of Chongzhen, reverently recorded with bowed head by Liu Qixiang, disciple of the bodhisattva precepts, formerly assistant prefect of Ruizhou in Jiangxi.
In Mourning for Chan Master Hanshan's Passing into Quiescence
Xiao Yunju (Junior Minister, a native of Guangxi)
In Mourning for the Great Monk Hanshan (with a preface)
Wu Zhongwei (Left Vice Commissioner, a native of Haiyan)

Master Hanshan was a dragon elephant of the Chan school. When I had charge of troops in Hunan, I was able to pay him a visit and make offerings. In the spring of the gengshen year I again filled a post beyond the ridges, and passing through Caoxi, I bowed in worship at Nanhua. The Patriarch's image barely kept off wind and rain; though great timbers lay piled like mountains, the work stood still with turtles sunning and cranes flying off, its colors peeling away. I paced back and forth a long while and sighed deeply. Asking how this had come about, an old bhikṣu answered, This is the unfinished work of our Great Master Hanshan. He sat in Chan for seven days, and the golden ground would have been completed; but slander built three evil paths, and the Dharma wheel halted midway. Having said this he choked and could not master his grief. I pitied his feeling and said to him, If you truly long for the Great Master, I shall summon him for you. The bhikṣu and the rest were all filled with immeasurable joy, threw themselves to the ground, and gave thanks. So I came a thousand li on blistered feet and earnestly extended the invitation. In such-and-such a month of that year he entered Caoxi a second time, and by then the monks had already invited the Great Master three times, and I too had sent him three letters. On the day his staff was planted, a Dharma message came to me. Bound by a petty office, I had no leisure to answer it in due course. I always thought that on some later day when I returned north I might at my ease visit the phantom city and look up to fathom the mind's truth. But his Dharma age was already full, and he suddenly entered parinirvāṇa, so what I had cherished for years became an empty hope. The vajra is indestructible, and so the great teaching flows on forever; but stone sparks cannot be prolonged, and so the flesh body comes to an end. I mourn that the ancestral wind is forever stilled; I grieve that the profound meaning is about to fall. Moved by the past, I am filled with sorrow; wounded by the present, I could die. Taking up my brush I have written this eulogy; my feeling shows itself in the words.
Passing Mt. Kuang, I Reverently Mourn Master Hanshan
Wang Siren (a native of Shanyin)

On the topmost peak of the seven peaks the ridges open;
when creepers and kudzu give out, only bare rock is left to climb.
The stream's tongue is so intricate it cannot be cut off,
and men still listen to Hanshan.

The ring was returned by the burning seas; the ruler's grace was great.
Crocodile waves and serpent clouds subdued how many demons.
Do not say that Vulture Peak came about through the power of the Way;
all that remains is his fair marks, to hear Amitābha.

A thousand preparations were made for one stupa;
how should one inquire at Caoxi and Mt. Lu?
Had I known that wind and moon would still be propped up,
when the one fire came there would have been nothing to carry.
In Mourning for the Great Master of Wuru
Dayi, a later student of Mt. Bo

Where the elephant king has walked, auspicious lotus opens;
before Wuru Peak his roar was like thunder.
Today why do the tree mists hang so thick and dim?
Purple clouds wheel in, pushed by the white clouds.
Lament for the Great Master of Wuru
His disciple Funeng

My memories of Nanhua are cut short; he has gone back and come no more.
How could I bear that he has already shed the old lotus womb?
Who among men has gained the marrow? It should be a laughing matter.
I have not forgotten my feeling, and so I must grieve.
Those who bear the Dharma from now on are all of feeble stuff;
of those who discussed its meaning in the past, how many were of heroic talent?
Pitiful is this lone traveler with only his two eyes,
gazing far at the green hills and weeping in the weeds.

I had just taken refuge at Twin Paths Mountain;
the master and his disciples come to mind, at ease on Vulture Peak.
How could the jade tree bear the blight on the green moss?
Even should the incense terrace return to its last road,
speech faced the stone spring and broke into sobs,
tears met the wind-blown leaves and fell in streams.
The Lankāvatāra Sūtra stands in four fascicles to seal the mind;
who is the man who has flung his arms free and gone out the gate?
A Letter Sent to the Dharma Heirs of Great Master Hanshan at Caoxi

Qian Qianyi, white-robed disciple of Haiyin, sends this letter to the Most Venerable Elder Brothers who are the resident masters of the stupa court of Great Master Hanshan at Caoxi.

With reverence: in the jiashen year the Great Master's true body was brought back to Caoxi from Wuru, and thirteen years have passed since then. I have repeatedly passed through death and disorder, escaping death ten thousand times; sight and breath barely remain, and I have shut myself away in the weeds. I could neither wrap my bundle and gird my bag to sweep the stupa court in person, nor compose my mind and bow in worship, sending from afar a single stick of incense. Above, I have failed in my toil for him; below, I have betrayed his bestowal of the prophecy. Bowing my head to the sky and treading upon the earth, my shame and sighing have no end. Yet having served him through many lives and taken refuge for a whole lifetime, I have not forgotten the seed of my former cause, nor ceased to long for my compassionate mother, like a child deprived of milk. This is a thing sea-ink could never exhaust, a thing the fire at the kalpa's end cannot burn away; and our Great Master must surely, within his long silent radiance, add pity and secretly bestow his blessing.

Since the Dharma banner toppled, the final kalpa has sunk ever lower: the lion has departed and the jackals howl; the dragons and elephants have lain down and the demon foxes blaze. Every household is Linji, every man a Deshan; masters of the school crowd like thatch, and transmitted whisks are as common as reeds. And beyond that they fabricate wild words and insult the holy monks. Slandering Zibo, they say he never had a transmission; reviling the Great Master, they say he merely spoke of doctrinal study. They gather the deaf and lead the blind, deluding the world and deceiving the people. The ruin of the Dharma gate has never been worse than at this time. The whole world drinks the drug of the mad well, and one man alone is not mad; the whole world dreads the head in the morning mirror, and one man alone does not dread. He stands alone, propping up a single pillar, with wind and snow at his gate. This one man — perhaps the Four World-Protecting Kings and the Adamantine Spirits of the Secret Truth use his hands as the Tathāgata's envoy, to sweep away demons and outsiders and not let the Buddha-seed be cut off. And our Great Master's compassionate heart, universally bestowing fearlessness, can hardly have had no deep hope for later men. Is that not so, Most Venerable Elders?

You and I differ as monastic and layman, yet we came forth from the same Master's gate and alike received his testament. Living in this age, to drift with the waves and follow the current, to sit and watch such men go raving like one struck by the wind, and to shake our hands and shut our eyes and not go to their rescue — how then can we be called true sons of Haiyin? The demons are strong and the Buddha weak; the worldly is heavy and the Way light; eyes of wisdom are few, and the Dharma city topples day by day. Will the Most Venerable Elders be able to laugh my words off as vast and empty?

What I urgently beg of your seats now is this. In recent times Zibo and Yunqi each have complete works circulating in the world. Of the Great Master's Dream-Journey Collection in the Jiaxing canon only one kind, the Dharma talks, is present; the rest — letters, records, prefaces, biographies, and the writings that elucidate the great Dharma — exist in title only, without the books themselves. I hear that the Master's surviving drafts are stored at Caoxi, and that the volumes are very rich. I make bold to request that they be poured out and given over. I shall collate their errors, cut away their redundancies, and let this world glimpse the whole jade disk, with no regret over half a pearl. They are the eye of gods and men, venerated throughout lands and dust-motes; by no means may this be long delayed, lest it bring the regret of being lost forever.

Further, the Master's Master Zuo's Mind-Method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that elucidates cause and effect. He often said that when he was cutting the draft at Caoxi, beneath the lamp and by the candle, searching out cases and judgments, his soul could be recalled and every hair stood on end. Given the season and conditions of this present age, the very time has come to reveal this book, to reform the stubborn and stop the slaughter, to fish up and gather this turbid kalpa. Thinking back on the Master's former entrustment, it was truly no casual matter. How can the duty of circulating it be evaded?

I bow and beg the Most Venerable Elders to join forces in searching and gathering, to collect with all your hearts, so that not a scrap of paper or a single word is missing. Strike the gavel, assemble the assembly, and proclaim it before the Great Master's true body; then lift it to the carriage, and let the imperial envoys send it by post with all solemnity, so that I may borrow their hands to compile and arrange it, and so bring the matter to completion. This is the shining light of a thousand autumns for the vehicle of Dharma and the ocean of teaching, not the private good fortune of one man at the gate.

I have presumptuously taken up the brush for the Wuru stupa court. Minister Chen of Nanhai once composed an inscription for it and had it carved in stone at Nanhua. For the affairs of the returning stupa after jiashen the mountain gate must have a true record. Not measuring my own crudeness, I wish to examine and compose a second stele, to complete the monastic history. I am seventy-five years old, and I vow that in the years left to me I shall take refuge in the Buddha's gate, reconcile the differences between the Tiantai and the worthy, break the partisan clinging of nature and marks, expound the bequeathed teaching, and protect the true vehicle, that I may in some small measure strain my remaining life and not fail the Great Master's supreme intent in rubbing my crown and entrusting me. When the collected works are finished and there is some first thread of order, I shall write a piece to announce it to the Great Master, secretly sensing his hidden response; my thoughts are here, ever here. But for now I have no leisure for it.

Gazing far toward the Twin Peaks, I burn incense and bow. The ridges and seas lie distant, yet he is as near as my mat and couch. The sky is cold and the night frozen; I chisel the ice and cut this tablet; my meaning is full but the paper is narrow, and I cannot say all I would. In the eleventh month of the bingshen year, three days before the winter solstice, I bow with joined palms and send up this letter.

The above is the letter by Qian Muzhai, Minister of Rites, seeking out the surviving drafts of Great Master Hanshan and commissioning Vice Censor-in-Chief Gong Xiaosheng to deliver. Recently he brought it to Haizhuang, and the Elder of Huashou looked at it, snapped his fingers, and bowed in praise. He was sighing that Master Qian could be true to his teacher, that Master Gong could be true to his friend, and that both were true to what the Buddha entrusted. He had it given to the printers, and commanded that I, Jinshi, write a colophon after it.

Alas, this Way has sunk low, and to the extreme in our day. It is all because the root of faith is shallow and slight, and men forget the source of Dharma and turn their backs on the Buddha's grace; toward the continuance or severance of the Wisdom-Life they act as though Yue were fat and Qin lean. Their laughter and their weeping are both false, and they rise and fall with other men. I beg to use this letter to admonish the descendants of the Dharma gate in the whole world and through ten thousand generations: know that the heart with which Master Qian did his utmost for the Great Master, the heart that Master Gong joined in protecting and spreading, and the heart that the Elder joined in circulating, all alike come forth from the heart of the great compassion and great vows of the Buddhas of the three ages. Where there is blood beneath the skin, a man hurts when touched, with not a thread between. His anxious tears already fall, and he forgets that to lose the self is no danger; thus the Wisdom-Life of the living and the Buddha truly leans and relies on it. How could it be no more than raising a bright Dharma banner for the Great Master? Written in the spring of the dingyou year, on the grain-god day of the first month, by the bhikṣu Jinshi, disciple of the Huashou gate.

Regarding your honor's instruction concerning the Complete Works of the Great Master Hanshan: I, Tai, am lodged in the government offices, and searching and inquiring for them is beyond my own power. Just now Jin Daoyin is here, and knows that the Vice Censor-in-Chief sent your honor's letter to the Dharma companions at Haizhuang. The abbot there, the Elder Zongbao, was joyful and full of praise; he burned incense and bowed, and commissioned Daoyin to write a colophon and send it to the printers, proclaiming it in every quarter, so that all who keep the Great Master's Dharma words, down to a single phrase or scrap of paper, may come and gather them. The several kinds at hand I send along in the Vice Censor-in-Chief's portmanteau; whatever else is obtained I, Tai, shall send on to you. Your disciple Wan Tai bows his head.
Old Preface to the Complete Works of Master Hanshan

I have often reflected on the sages and worthies who sustain the world. Establishing themselves in one generation, some create, some continue, some preserve what is complete, some revive what has fallen, some rescue it from corruption. In the subtlety of their work they leave nothing unprovided and no meaning unfulfilled, so that men a thousand myriad generations later who can seek out their purport may all rise up by means of it. Are these not the great constants and great laws of past and present? And then, going further, I reflect: if the sages and worthies who sustain the world can still, with their own persons, exhaust the affairs of one generation and, with the Way, open the hearts of ten thousand generations, how much more can our Buddha and Patriarchs, who appear in the world for men's sake, using the Dharma that transcends birth and death and the nature, transform the hearts of ordinary and holy, deluded and awakened? In their manifestation of the universal gate and their response to beings of different kinds, how could they fail to continue the lamp of wisdom of the three ages and transmit the all-knowing wisdom of the great chiliocosm? This I have seen in Great Master Hanshan.

The Master's gate of awakening and the vastness of his teaching are already seen in his own writings and in the fullness of the biographies and praise-inscriptions by men of clear eye, so that the whole world knows him for a flesh-body mahāsattva come again. What word of praise can I add? It is because I grieve for the Dharma gate that I am moved to feeling.

At the time when the Chan gate was declining, the Master stood as a tripod with the two Great Masters Yunqi and Daguan. Though he had awakened to the Chan gate, he did not occupy the seat of the Chan gate: he foreknew that the Chan gate would revive, and so he made a great bulwark for it, deliberately leaving that seat empty and honoring that school, so that the wild and presumptuous, the usurping and thieving, would themselves feel fear and not dare to look on it lightly or hold it cheap. Was his heart any less than that of Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu? Alas, with three Great Masters shining so brightly before them, later ages still produced usurpers who did not scruple to be the Master's criminals. Is this not matter for deep sighing?

Still, when Confucius made the Spring and Autumn Annals, he set right the names and duties of ten thousand generations. Though he could not make the names and duties of ten thousand generations all correct, yet those who cannot set names and duties right — how can they escape the condemnation of the Spring and Autumn? In former years I saw the Master's praise of my ancestor of Shouchang and the stupa inscription he composed for him, in which the lines stood out, How grand is this great mountain; a thousand li apart we meet from afar, and I already knew that he and my ancestor walked hand in hand along the road that goes beyond. As for the Dharma he spoke and the works he wrote in his life, they bend to the utmost to the teaching of one age, from first to last, root and branch, wholly the Buddha's mind and wholly the Patriarchs' intent. How are his raised phrases and capping verses, his pointing instructions in verse, any less than the ancients', or yielding to those of today? The world and later ages will of themselves know that the Master was in truth a man of the Patriarchal seat who did not occupy it. How could one take his not occupying it as proof that he was not a man of the Patriarchal seat? Twenty-two years after the Master's death his whole body is undecayed, and with the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, who created and revived, there is no second meaning. Advancing to the great constants and great laws that sustain the world, and able to continue the Wisdom-Life of the Dharma-body, truly there is nothing he did not provide and nothing he did not fulfill.

Now the Master's Dharma grandson Jianru wishes to raise subscriptions to print the Master's complete works, and has specially asked me for a preface to approve and assist it. I admire his sincerity in forgetting his own body for the Dharma, and so I have set down the thoughts of admiration and deep feeling that I hold. Reverently inscribed by the later student Daosheng of Tianjie.
Introduction to Master Hanshan's Oral Raft

Last year Vice Censor-in-Chief Gong Xiaosheng went to Guangdong, and Minister Qian of Yushan entrusted him with collecting the surviving writings of Great Master Hanshan. At that time the Elder of Huashou and the monk Qihe of Dinghu gathered the Dharma talks and various discourses and sent them along with the envoy's carriage to Zhuhai, so that the light of the Mani pearl already shone upon the hills of Wu and the waters of Zhe.

From my friend Huang Qiuwen I obtained one more piece of his last words: what he spoke to the student Deng Fu when he was reviving the ancestral court of Caoxi, the so-called Oral Raft. The Master spoke the Dharma as it came from his mouth, and the brush in his hand ran to a thousand words without a single correction, all flowing out from the inconceivable. In what he showed to student Deng, his pointing words beneath the words ran through and pierced in every direction; never has there been a single direct pointing so simple, swift, and piercing as this.

The Master, with Yunqi and Zibo, were called the three great masters of the same time, and Hong was himself personally granted the prophecy. Yunqi did the Buddha's work with lowered brows; the Master and Zibo did the Buddha's work with glaring eyes. Yet their devices mostly came out of the water contemplation of Mt. Wutai, and so whatever their paper and ink proclaimed invariably carried the heroic grandeur of a thousand peaks of piled snow and ten thousand gorges of rolling thunder. In this scrap of paper one may glimpse a corner of it.

When it is printed I shall still send it to the Minister, so that he may add it to the complete works, and I reverently write a few words after it. In the fifth month of the dingyou year, Zeng Hong of Zhongzhou speaks with joined palms.
